en: If caught outside during a thunderstorm, crouch low with your feet together to minimize your contact with the ground and avoid lightning strikes.
During an earthquake, practice the Drop, Cover, and Hold on technique under a sturdy desk to protect your head and neck from falling debris.
Always wear thick gloves when handling soil because it can contain Clostridium tetani bacteria, which causes tetanus if it enters a cut on your skin.
Boiling floodwater or tap water for at least one minute kills harmful bacteria and parasites, making it safe to drink during a typhoon.
The Sun emits ultraviolet radiation that can damage your skin and eyes, so wearing sunscreen and sunglasses protects you during outdoor recess.
High humidity during the wet season reduces sweat evaporation, increasing your risk of heatstroke, so drink plenty of water and rest in the shade.
During a full moon, stronger gravitational pull causes higher spring tides, so always check local tide warnings before swimming at the beach at night.
When a volcano like Taal erupts, wear an N95 mask and goggles to prevent fine volcanic ash from irritating your lungs and eyes.
A storm surge pushes seawater inland during a typhoon, so always evacuate to higher ground immediately if local authorities issue a surge warning.
Planting deep-rooted vetiver grass on steep hillsides stabilizes the soil and prevents deadly landslides from occurring during heavy monsoon rains.
After heavy rainfall, empty any stagnant water in old tires or cans to stop Aedes aegypti mosquitoes from breeding and spreading dengue fever.
The mineral fluorite is the source of fluoride, which dentists add to toothpaste to strengthen your tooth enamel and prevent painful cavities.
